evaluation.positioning_hook: In plague-shadowed Roman Hispania, a feared exorcist and a skeptical young librarian race to expose a family’s hidden crime before a militarized city turns them into the next public enemies.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is vivid and the exorcism frame gives it an easy genre read, but the script’s dense, literary dialogue and historical setting narrow the commercial lane. It feels more like a specialty prestige buy than a broad four-quadrant play.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands early: a legendary exorcist, a sick girl, a suspicious family, and Roman authority closing in. The complication is that the script keeps re-framing the mystery through flashbacks and philosophical exchanges, which blunts the clean elevator pitch.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Evano has a strong silhouette — controlled, severe, and intellectually theatrical — and Aragon gives the story a younger, more accessible point of entry. The supporting cast is colorful, but several characters function more as puzzle pieces than fully durable personalities.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s Roman exorcist premise, scientific-method exorcism language, and plague-era paranoia create a distinctive mash-up. It’s bold in texture and vocabulary, even when the underlying mystery mechanics are more familiar.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story has a clear engine — identify the real cause of the possession and survive the Roman response — and the cemetery reveal gives it a strong late push. But the long scenic detours and repeated explanatory passages slow the forward drive.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The exorcist is not just a priestly figure but a forensic, almost detective-like operator in a Roman political nightmare, which gives the premise a fresh center. The reveal that the “possession” is a cover for family murder and trauma lands as both surprising and thematically coherent.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Rome, Hispania, the army, the crows, the plague fear, and the city’s social hierarchy all feel story-generating rather than decorative. The world has rules and pressure points, though the script sometimes explains its mythology more than it dramatizes it.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unusually ornate: biblical, political, and noir-ish, with a self-conscious literary cadence. That voice is distinctive, though it can feel more declared than fully controlled in the dialogue.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There’s real subtext around fear, authority, guilt, and the stories societies tell to survive trauma. The Exorcist’s Rome-bound destination and the repeated references to prior encounters suggest a larger mythic world beyond this one case.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Evano and Aragon form a workable central duo, and the family/city/army triangle gives the script recurring friction. Still, most relationships are functional rather than combustible, so the ensemble energy is narrower than the world suggests.

lead_characters.name: Evano D'Asmodeo
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s-50s, Italian, outsider/intellectual, physically controlled, emotionally guarded.
lead_characters.hook: A scarred Italian doctor known as the Exorcist, Evano is a coldly brilliant investigator who treats possession like a solvable case and people like evidence. He speaks in riddles, moves with authority, and carries the burden of a past that clearly made him both feared and indispensable.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Mads Mikkelsen in The Hunt or Javier Bardem in No Country for Old Men — a severe, magnetic presence whose stillness becomes the performance. The role gives an actor authority, menace, and philosophical command in the same frame.

lead_characters.name: Aragon
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late teens to 20s, Hispania, literate, working-class, observant.
lead_characters.hook: A young librarian from a starving town, Aragon is the audience’s entry point: skeptical, hungry, proud, and increasingly pulled into Evano’s orbit. He starts as a question-asker and ends up as a moral witness to the exorcist’s method.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Timothée Chalamet in Beautiful Boy or Lucas Hedges in Manchester by the Sea a chance to play intelligence under pressure. It offers a young actor a reactive, emotionally legible arc with room for wonder and dread.

lead_characters.name: Fresno
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s-50s, father, husband, local citizen of Cartaeia.
lead_characters.hook: Fresno presents as a desperate father protecting a sick child, but he’s actually the story’s hidden engine of guilt and deception. He weaponizes superstition, grief, and civic panic to conceal a murder and keep the town from looking too closely.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong supporting-villain territory in the vein of Michael Shannon in Revolutionary Road or Ben Mendelsohn in Animal Kingdom — a man whose panic curdles into control. The role gives an actor a slow reveal from concern to monstrous self-preservation.

lead_characters.name: Donna
lead_characters.demographics: Female, early teens, Hispania, child/young teen, emotionally fractured.
lead_characters.hook: Donna is the split identity at the center of the family trauma: one self protective and functional, the other trapped in the memory of violence. She’s the script’s most vulnerable emotional vessel, carrying the aftermath of what the adults have buried.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of psychologically layered young role that made Saoirse Ronan in Atonement or Brooklynn Prince in The Florida Project unforgettable. It offers a child actor a rare chance to play fear, dissociation, and innocence without sentimentality.

lead_characters.name: Juliana
lead_characters.demographics: Female, around 11, child, sickly, physically vulnerable.
lead_characters.hook: Juliana is the apparent possession case, but the script uses her body as the site where the family’s lie becomes visible. She’s less a conventional character than a crucial dramatic pressure point whose illness exposes the truth.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a high-impact child role in the tradition of Linda Blair in The Exorcist — a performance built on physical transformation and audience dread. It’s the kind of part that can define a young actor’s early career if handled with precision.

lead_characters.name: General Spurius
lead_characters.hook: General Spurius is the face of Rome’s coercive power: disciplined, punitive, and ideologically absolute. He doesn’t just hunt Evano; he represents the state’s appetite for control and public example.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is classic commanding-antagonist material in the lane of Ralph Fiennes in Schindler’s List or Mark Strong in Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy. The role gives an actor clipped authority, menace, and institutional power.

lead_characters.name: Salamandra
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 30s-50s, former singer, local celebrity, alcoholic, socially magnetic.
lead_characters.hook: Salamandra is the bar’s seductive ghost of a better past: witty, damaged, and still capable of reading a room faster than anyone else. She carries the town’s memory in her body and becomes one of the story’s most tragic witnesses.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do what Frances McDormand did in Three Billboards or Penélope Cruz in Volver — charisma, pain, and lived-in authority. It’s a late-scene-stealing part with real emotional residue.

lead_characters.name: Driugo
lead_characters.hook: Driugo is the town’s keeper of the dead, and his cowardice is what allows the lie to harden into history. He’s not a mastermind so much as a man who chose fear over truth and now has to stand in the wreckage.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of morally compromised supporting role that gives an actor the same grim payoff as John Hawkes in Winter’s Bone or Richard Jenkins in The Visitor. It’s a guilt-heavy part with a strong final reckoning.

lead_characters.name: Ajax
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late teens to 20s, Roman-aligned youth, physically capable.
lead_characters.hook: Ajax is the next generation of Rome’s violence: eager, impressionable, and desperate to be seen as worthy by the system that will use him. His final turn makes him a chilling emblem of inherited obedience.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a breakout-supporting role in the vein of Barry Keoghan in Dunkirk or Harris Dickinson in The King’s Man — youthful, dangerous, and emotionally conflicted. It gives an actor a sharp turn from innocence to complicity.

casting_characteristics: One child role with major emotional weight
One early-teen role with psychological complexity
Strong age-specific supporting roles for Roman authority and local townspeople

notable_requirements: Cemetery with tomb and burial site

technical.vfx_details: Primarily atmospheric work: crows, smoke, blood, and a few stylized visual transitions between time periods.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical blood, knife wound effects, candle/fire effects, trunk/tomb burial action, and corpse/illness makeup.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Realistic release model is specialty theatrical or prestige streaming feature; the material is adult, historical, and dialogue-driven.

budget.note: The period setting, Roman crowd scenes, forest build, cemetery work, and costume requirements push this above a contained indie, even though the VFX and stunt load stay modest.

casting.note: Evano needs a very specific blend of intellectual authority, menace, and spiritual gravitas, while Donna and Juliana require age-sensitive child casting with emotional precision.

development.note: The script’s mystery is clear, but the dense dialogue, flashback structure, and mythic language will need a buyer comfortable with a literary historical register.

comp_set.title: The Name of the Rose
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the historical-investigative lane, the intellectual detective figure, and the sense of religious authority colliding with hidden crime.

comp_set.title: The Exorcist
comp_set.why_it_comps: Not in budget scale, but in premise DNA: a possession framework that masks a deeper spiritual and bodily crisis.

comp_set.title: The Seventh Seal
comp_set.why_it_comps: The philosophical, death-haunted register and the medieval/ancient moral atmosphere echo the script’s baroque seriousness.

comp_set.title: Agora
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the historical setting, civic unrest, and the collision between belief systems and public power.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adult viewers who like historical mysteries with religious dread, moral ambiguity, and elevated dialogue.
audience_target.demographics: 35+, skewing cinephile and prestige-drama friendly, with strongest pull among viewers who respond to literary genre material.

budget_tier.note: Period costumes, Roman crowd moments, and multiple historical locations keep this in the specialty indie range despite the modest effects load.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally with buyers looking for elevated genre material that can play festivals, attract strong actors, and sell on concept plus tone rather than spectacle. The script’s historical specificity and exorcism frame give it a clean marketing angle for adult audiences.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature: Evano is vivid, but the supporting cast and world do not yet present a clear spinoff vector with separate franchise value.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The exorcist is a detective, not a priest.
strengths.what_it_means: That reframes a familiar supernatural lane into a procedural-investigation engine, which is easier to market than pure mysticism and gives the buyer a clean protagonist function. It will appeal to actors and directors who want genre material with intellectual authority rather than standard horror mechanics.
strengths.evidence: Evano repeatedly uses observation, experimentation, and proof to diagnose Juliana’s case and expose Fresno’s lie.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The Roman setting generates real pressure.
strengths.what_it_means: The army, public fear, and civic hierarchy create a built-in external antagonist that keeps the story from feeling like a closed-room occult puzzle. That makes the project more attractive to buyers who want historical texture that actively drives plot.
strengths.evidence: General Spurius hunts Evano, soldiers move through the city, and the crowd turns on anyone linked to the Exorcist.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The family reveal lands as tragedy, not gimmick.
strengths.what_it_means: The possession setup resolves into murder, trauma, and dissociation, which gives the climax emotional weight beyond the genre reveal. That kind of turn helps a prestige buyer justify the material as more than a one-note exorcism story.
strengths.evidence: Fresno killed his wife, hid the body, and used the “pest” story to cover the truth while Donna/Francesca fractures under the memory.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Evano has a strong star silhouette.
strengths.what_it_means: The role is built around authority, restraint, and verbal dominance, which is exactly the kind of part that can attract a serious actor looking for a signature genre turn. That gives the package a real anchor even before the rest of the cast is attached.
strengths.evidence: Evano’s entrances, his controlled interrogation style, and his final exorcism speech all position him as the story’s gravitational center.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The script has a distinctive literary voice.
strengths.what_it_means: The dialogue and narration create a baroque identity that separates the project from standard exorcism fare and gives marketing a tonal hook. Buyers looking for elevated, authorial genre material will recognize that immediately.
strengths.evidence: The script repeatedly uses aphorisms, moral pronouncements, and philosophical monologues about dust, crows, devils, and proof.

whats_special.headline: This is a prestige historical mystery with a genre engine: a forensic exorcist, a Roman city under pressure, and a family secret that turns possession into murder. The period footprint is real but manageable, and the lead role is the kind of star vehicle that can open a specialty package fast.

items.area: The dialogue carries more weight than the scenes.
items.detail: A lot of the script’s momentum comes from speeches about proof, dust, devils, and cowardice rather than from reversals or action beats. That gives the piece a strong literary identity, but it also narrows the audience to buyers comfortable with a highly verbal historical register.

items.area: The flashback structure slows the mystery.
items.detail: The script keeps jumping between the Rome/Hispania present and earlier Terragonia material, which spreads the reveal across multiple timelines. A producer will notice the risk that the central question gets diluted before the cemetery payoff arrives.

items.area: The supporting cast is vivid but unevenly dimensional.
items.detail: Evano and Fresno are sharply defined, but several supporting figures — including Aragon, Driugo, and General Spurius — function more as thematic instruments than fully surprising people. That matters because the script’s world is strong enough to invite richer relationship play than it currently delivers.

items.area: The period setting keeps the buyer pool specialized.
items.detail: Roman Hispania, military costumes, and historical crowd scenes make this a specialty play rather than a broad commercial feature. That is fine for the right lane, but it means the package needs a buyer who actively wants elevated historical genre material.

issues.headline: The main friction is not concept but register: this is a dense, speech-forward historical mystery that will play best for prestige buyers, not broad commercial ones. The other watchout is structural — the flashback-heavy reveal path and the supporting cast’s limited dimensionality keep the script from fully cashing the richness of its world.
